1. Scope

Construct one independent internal geometry whose solved standing waves have reproducible, readable distinctions that persist under the stated isolated dynamics. The proposed particle-type identifier is the occupied standing-mode sector of a nonzero pure-mode preparation. General superpositions remain allowed and receive a modal-energy signature rather than an invented single type.

The physical system is one real scalar internal wave on a bounded interval. Both ends are fixed. A specified local clock measures its evolution. An internal profile and its rate of change define the complete state. A separately prescribed influence is introduced only to calculate the interface conditions for a later transition.

Obligation Required endpoint
O1 — Geometry Domain, dimension, topology, metric, measure, fields, boundaries and every scale are explicit.
O2 — Solved waves Derive the complete mode family, distinguish at least two solutions and calculate the available count.
O3 — Readout and persistence Compute an operational type readout from the complete state and prove its isolated persistence.
O4 — Energy and stability Calculate energy, current, preparation-dependent differences and the precise stability statement.
O5 — Numerical anchors Identify every constant, convention, preparation and functional input, with an anchor and a fixing procedure.
O6 — Transition interface Give the work and modal-coupling conditions that a physical change of type must satisfy.
O7 — Completion Supply reproducible numerical examples, actual checks and a precise mathematical verdict.

The scope does not require a preassigned species count, a generation count, a mass table, another attribute’s geometry, a quantum evolution law, a quantization rule or a complete weak interaction. Granularity and collapse remain separately numbered tasks. A finite species count is not assumed. No external spatial embedding, equality of internal and external propagation speeds, or identification of an action with Planck’s constant is imported.

The result is a candidate flavor mechanism under the physical identification in P4. Its mathematical content is the solved geometry, distinguishability, conserved modal data and transition accounting. Physical calibration status is stated in Section 3.

2. Method

The backward plan starts with a persistent, distinguishable type readout. It requires distinguishable stable mode sectors, which require a specified boundary-value problem and an evolution that preserves those sectors. A positive local quadratic wave action on a fixed interval is a sufficient completion. It is selected for this construction, then solved; it is not claimed to be the unique geometry allowed by the target.

There is one primary candidate and a finite set of checks. No fallback was needed. The calculation uses exact separation, projection, integration and energy identities before its numerical examples. The explicit coupling profile is a bounded interface diagnostic, not execution of the later force step.

Stage Inputs and operation Completion and check
Geometry Fix the interval, scalar values, metric, measure and endpoints. Every geometric quantity is specified; coordinate conversion is checked.
Evolution Vary the stated action with the stated boundaries. Wave equation and local energy current follow with their coefficients.
Modes Solve the boundary problem and normalize its solutions. Spectrum, multiplicity and complete finite-energy expansion are obtained.
Readout Project both displacement and velocity onto the calculated profiles. Pure type, vacuum and mixtures are distinguished through every phase.
Persistence Evolve the projected amplitudes and compare difference solutions. Modal energies and the perturbation-energy norm are conserved.
Energy comparison Declare which preparation quantity is held fixed. General differences and matched-action examples have explicit formulas.
Interface Add a typed source or a specified overlap profile. Work, selection coefficients and total-balance conditions are calculated.
Numerical example Fix all model-unit inputs, then evaluate the finite verification set. The actual results appear in Section 7.

Thought experiment A — distinguish two preparations. In the same internal geometry and with the same clock, prepare the first and second standing modes separately. Read the complete field state with the defined projection procedure. Their profiles, nodal patterns and temporal frequencies differ. The numerical comparison specifies equal modal action, so their energy difference is calculated from a declared preparation.

Thought experiment B — observe a zero crossing. Wait until the whole displacement profile of a pure standing wave is zero. Its velocity profile is then nonzero. Reading both components preserves the type label; reading displacement alone would mistake this state for vacuum.

Thought experiment C — apply a specified influence. Start in one pure mode and switch on the explicitly defined internal profile. A previously empty adjacent mode has a calculated nonzero initial acceleration. The influence changes the state through an equation of motion. Merely renaming the original mode would leave every projection unchanged.

All three experiments use the same interval and local clock. The source in C is a prescribed participant whose supplied work is included in the balance.

Geometry and numerical inputs

The internal domain has one real coordinate and two boundary points. The wave value is one real number. Mode coefficients are mathematical readout data. None of these is ordinary external position or a combined space containing charge, spin or another attribute.

The panel specifies the full geometry and the seven-column constants-and-anchors register. It distinguishes physical scale parameters, coordinate and amplitude conventions, preparation data, functional inputs and numerical settings.

FG1 — Typed geometry and state variables.

The interval is a compact connected one-dimensional manifold with boundary. It has one global arclength chart, no coordinate identifications and no chart transitions. The chosen coordinate runs from the labeled left endpoint to the labeled right endpoint. Reversing that orientation does not change the mode number. The field-value comparison is ordinary real multiplication. There is no independently chosen field-space metric parameter.

The dimensionless chart does not remove the geometric length: it moves the length into the metric and wave equation. In arclength coordinates the connection coefficient is zero. Intrinsic curvature is zero for this one-dimensional metric; no extrinsic embedding or additional curvature field is used by this construction.

The exact material statements are

These are the regularity conditions for the driven energy identity and the pointwise coefficient-work formula. The isolated construction has zero drive. The modal symbol denotes a field projection, not electric charge.

Here the field is dimensionless by convention. If energy, time and internal length units are denoted by E, T and L, then the action has units E·T, the coefficient has units E·T², the internal speed has units L/T, and the generalized drive has units E. This coefficient is a wave-storage normalization; its name does not execute the separate inertia-space task.

Appendix P1 — Bounded geometry and geometric admissibility

Status: selected internal interval and clock; its normalized profiles and geometric relations are calculated. Used by O1–O2.

The domain, arclength metric and endpoints in P1 are a sufficient bounded geometry for standing waves. They are not inferred from the existence of observed particle types. The local wave action in P2 makes the spatial equation relevant; the fixed ends in P3 close its boundary problem.

For a separated nonzero profile, integration by parts gives

The strict inequality holds because a zero-derivative profile would be constant and the two fixed endpoints would make it zero. Thus the nontrivial sector has positive spatial frequency. The general solution is a linear combination of sine and cosine. The left endpoint removes the cosine term; the right endpoint requires an integer number of half wavelengths. Each admissible spatial eigenspace is one-dimensional over the reals.

The normalized pairing follows directly from product-to-sum integration:

The profile has exactly one fewer interior nodes than its positive mode index, except that the entire displacement can vanish at a temporal zero crossing. The label itself is unchanged by reflecting the coordinate; the profile’s parity and sign change do not convert one mode into another.

The local metric and normalized measure are mutually consistent:

No periodic identification, additional shape function or boundary stiffness remains unspecified. The length is the one geometric scale. Smoothness of the displayed modes is explicit; the full weak domain is treated in P3.

Status: selected positive local quadratic dynamics. Its equation of motion and balance law are derived. Used by O2–O4.

The variation vanishes at the initial/final variation times and at the fixed interval endpoints. Starting from P2’s displayed action, the integrations by parts are

The temporal boundary term vanishes by the variation convention. The spatial term is proportional to the endpoint value of the variation and vanishes by P3. No quantum equation is used.

Positive temporal and gradient storage are a sufficient classical choice that yields a bounded free energy and an exactly solvable standing-wave problem. Other dynamics are not excluded by this choice, but they would define a different construction.

For smooth fields, direct differentiation gives

The last equality uses a smooth fixed-end solution: the endpoint displacement is zero at every time, so its time derivative is zero there. In units, the density has energy per internal length and the current has energy per time. The normalized measure has not lost a factor of the interval length.

A real standing mode may have an instantaneous internal energy current, but it has fixed spatial nodes and no one-way translating profile. Its current is

This vanishes at both endpoints and has zero time average at every interior point. “Standing” does not mean that energy never redistributes within the standing pattern.

Appendix P3 — Complete spectrum, finite-energy evolution and stability

Status: stated boundary and energy domain; completeness, conservation and stability are proved in that domain. Used by O2–O4.

To justify completeness, scale to the unit interval and extend a square-integrable function oddly to a two-periodic function. The odd Fourier sector consists exactly of the sine profiles. A brief proof of the Fourier completeness statement used here is supplied by the Fejér kernels. On the two-periodic coordinate, define

The removable values at integer periods are filled continuously. The kernels are nonnegative, and their mass outside any fixed neighborhood of zero tends to zero: the denominator is bounded away from zero there and the numerator is bounded, leaving a bound proportional to the reciprocal of the order. Convolution with this normalized kernel is a finite trigonometric polynomial. Translation continuity in square-integrable norm and the triangle inequality give

Split the integral into a small neighborhood, where translation continuity makes the norm difference small, and its complement, whose kernel mass tends to zero. Translation continuity follows first for continuous periodic functions by uniform continuity and then for square-integrable functions by their norm approximation with continuous functions. Consequently a function orthogonal to every Fourier mode is zero; the odd sector gives completeness of the sine profiles. For zero-trace displacement in the first Sobolev space, the odd periodic extension also has a square-integrable weak derivative. The same approximation applied to that derivative gives convergence in the required energy norm. This supplies the exact completeness form used here.

Parseval and integration by parts therefore give

Every finite partial sum is a smooth solution with conserved energy. Its tail energy is time independent and tends to zero as the truncation is removed. The partial sums thus converge in the energy-state norm, defining the unique weak solution with the stated initial data. Conservation passes to that limit. This avoids assigning pointwise endpoint fluxes to rough fields that do not have the needed classical traces.

The available nonzero standing profiles are indexed by all positive integers. There is one spatial profile per index, with arbitrary real temporal phase and amplitude. This is a countably infinite family of type sectors, not a three- or six-species conclusion.

For any positive finite energy ceiling, every index still has a nonzero allowed preparation: choose its amplitude inversely proportional to its frequency. Thus neither finite energy nor finite interval length alone makes the mode count finite.

A frequency-limited readout has a different, explicitly conditional count:

Below the first frequency the count is zero. This is a count within a specified readout band; it is not a law excluding higher-frequency states.

For two isolated solutions, let their difference be the complete state

Linearity makes the difference another solution, hence

The Dirichlet bound follows directly from the modal sum:

Thus small energy-state perturbations remain small. A pure-mode state perturbed by off-mode content is a mixture; stability does not turn that mixture back into an exact pure type. The modal-energy content of the mixture also stays constant under isolated evolution. No attraction to one mode is asserted.

Appendix P4 — A readable type, including zero crossings and mixtures

Status: the particle-type interpretation is explicit. The distinction and its persistence are calculated from the full wave state. Used by O3.

The projections implement an actual readout operation on the defined complete state: compare the field and its rate with each normalized profile and integrate in the stated measure. They are geometric comparisons and integrals, not inherited quantum observable rules. For pure mode data the calculation returns the prepared amplitude in exactly one sector and zero in the others.

The countable ideal signature is an exact mathematical readout. An actual finite-band instrument must state its bandwidth and tolerance; content above its band is unresolved, not proved absent. The worked preparations have finitely known mode support, so their exact signature is determined by the displayed integrals.

At a turning point the roles reverse. Only simultaneous zero displacement and zero velocity in every sector is vacuum. The modal radius is phase-independent:

For a general nonzero state define the full classical signature

These are energy shares, not probabilities or a collapse law. Assigning the pure-mode label to every mixture would be a change of definition with no supporting mechanism. An operational classifier may separately report a dominant mode under a declared tolerance, without calling the mixed state pure.

For example, a conservative sufficient tolerance bound follows from orthogonality. If the initial pure state has energy-state norm , and a perturbation has norm at most with , then

The original mode carries more energy than all other modes together. That dominance persists because each modal energy is conserved. This is a robust readout statement about a mixture, not an assertion of exact pure-mode robustness under arbitrary perturbations.

The physical proposal is that an independently prepared pure sector can serve as a particle-type distinction. The scalar standing-wave mathematics proves distinguishability and isolated persistence; P4 supplies the interpretation.

The general energy difference depends on both mode and preparation. It is not a fixed gap determined by the integer label alone.

Appendix P6 — A real transition needs a coupling and work account

Status: explicitly supplied influence; exact geometric comparison and balance identities. Used by O6.

The additive generalized drive has energy units in the normalized measure. The coefficient in front of the acceleration is essential for the displayed work identity. At smooth fixed ends the boundary term is zero. For weak solutions take the drive locally integrable in time with values in the stated square-integrable field space; the integrated balance follows by the energy-space limit. The numerical interface examples use finite smooth sums. The coefficient is continuously differentiable where its pointwise work formula is used.

The exact complete balance is

For constant coefficient, the sum of free wave energy and interaction storage is conserved. For a time-dependent coefficient, the right-hand side is the explicit power supplied by the participant controlling that coefficient. Integrating it supplies the work account. Calling the free wave energy alone conserved during this driven process would omit the declared source and interaction.

If both the additive source and the overlap influence are present, their terms combine in the same balance:

The symmetry of the matrix makes the cancellation exact: differentiate the interaction quadratic form, use the modal equations, and cancel its terms linear in the modal velocities. This proof holds for finite smooth sums and extends where the displayed energy and bounded multiplication form are defined.

Since the magnitude of the cosine profile never exceeds one, the complete quadratic energy has the sufficient lower bound

Here the Dirichlet bound was used for the gradient term. A stronger comparison with the free energy is

Thus a coefficient with magnitude strictly below the squared first frequency gives positive storage equivalent to the free energy form. This is a sufficient positivity domain. For a constant coefficient, the conserved positive Hamiltonian also controls perturbations in the energy norm. A time-dependent coefficient can supply energy through the displayed work term, so positivity alone does not establish dynamical stability for that driven case.

For a putative pure-to-pure conversion, the source and interaction must also meet endpoint conditions. If the interaction is off at both endpoints, and the same fixed ends admit no flux, then

For matched-action endpoints that difference is the one in FG9. The actual source must also empty every unwanted final mode and prepare the required phase and amplitude. A nonzero overlap coefficient by itself does not prove that an arbitrary desired endpoint can be reached. This construction exports the equations and balance to be satisfied; it does not assign a weak-interaction rate, collapse event or particle-decay law.

7. Definition of completeness and finite tests

The present step is complete when the geometry and dynamics are explicit, at least two nonzero distinguishable standing waves are solved, their readout and persistence are established in a defined domain, the available count is derived, energy and stability are checked, all numerical inputs have fixing procedures, and the transition interface states its actual work and coupling conditions.

The result has three distinct completion levels: the parameterized mathematical construction is complete; the numerical example is fully specified; physical calibration has the status recorded in Section 3. A six-species selection, full particle catalogue, force law or collapse mechanism is not a completion test of this step.

8. Summaries for three audiences

For a child

We gave a hidden wave a small line with two fixed ends. It can make different standing patterns: one bump, two alternating bumps, three, and more. Each pattern has its own rhythm. We wrote down a way to tell the patterns apart even at the instant when the line looks flat, because it can still be moving.

Under the chosen rules, a pattern prepared by itself keeps its identity. A mixture keeps a record of how much energy belongs to each pattern. We propose using a pure pattern’s identity as a kind of particle type. The examples show the calculation works; they do not assign the patterns to named real particles. To change patterns, something must actually act on the wave and account for the energy.

These statements are the same wave and readout proofs in Appendices P1–P4, with the physical identification in P4.

For a physics teacher

The construction chooses a real scalar field on a fixed-end interval with a positive classical wave action. Its sine spectrum is discrete and nondegenerate, while amplitudes and phases remain continuous. Projection of both field and velocity gives conserved modal energies and a phase-safe readout. A nonzero single mode supplies the proposed type distinction; a superposition has its full modal signature.

The complete state’s energy norm is conserved, so the isolated evolution is stable in that sense. There are infinitely many admitted profiles. Equal action, equal amplitude and equal energy are different preparations and produce different comparisons. The supplied cosine influence has an explicitly calculated adjacent-mode overlap and a complete work balance. Geometry, anchors, premise foundations and verification are all stated before the worked examples.

The first line is derived from P1–P3. The energy comparison uses P5; the comparison matrix uses P6’s specified profile. See FG6–FG12.

For a theoretical physicist

The sufficient model is a real Dirichlet wave on a metric interval with normalized arclength measure and a positive energy form on the real energy phase space. Its simple discrete spatial spectrum supplies invariant pure-mode sectors, with the proposed flavor interpretation stated independently. Fourier completeness and the tail-energy argument extend the modal conservation law to finite-energy data. The phase-space readout distinguishes pure sectors, mixtures and vacuum.

The classical action comparison exposes the preparation dependence of energy differences. The count is unbounded unless an additional stated restriction is imposed. A bounded multiplicative profile gives a derived sparse comparison matrix and exact driven work identity. Calibration separates the speed/length ratio, field normalization and energy scale. No granularity, quantum probability rule or species representation is inherited.

The quadratic form notation is shorthand for the explicit integrals and convergent/modal sums in Appendix P6; it does not prescribe a quantum observable or a combined internal ontology.

10. What distinguishes the types, and what changes them

Three directly calculated features distinguish a prepared pure sector: its standing profile, its nodal structure and its proper-clock frequency. The projection readout combines the field and its velocity so that a temporal zero crossing does not erase the distinction. A global sign reversal or a time shift changes phase within the same type. A spatial coordinate reflection changes parity within the same index.

A mixed state retains multiple modal energy shares. The isolated equation preserves all of them. Thus it preserves an already pure type and does not manufacture purity from a mixture.

The displayed overlap profile can transfer energy between modal components. Its nonzero comparison coefficients calculate which components are directly connected by that profile. Completing a pure-to-pure transition would additionally require a source history and verified endpoint conditions. Those conditions are exported explicitly.

The computed invariant signature is

Two profiles with different positive indices are orthogonal. Their temporal frequencies differ because the internal speed and interval length are positive. Hence their distinctions are not produced merely by assigning different names.

For the chosen overlap diagnostic,

The isolated equation is recovered by setting the supplied coefficient to zero. At the initial time of a first-mode preparation, the second-mode acceleration follows from this equation, while a relabeling would leave every amplitude unchanged.

The additional numerical calculation uses a declared finite projection of these equations. The full analytical comparison and work identities are independent of that numerical projection; its truncation is not a physical boundary on the available modes.

The energy anchor fixes the storage coefficient only after the field-amplitude convention is declared. The preparation amplitude and phase are then fixed by two initial quadratures or the selected action and a phase choice.

These are finite inverse procedures. They retain symbolic values when the required anchor data are absent and do not start a further derivation of unit standards.

14. Mathematical verdict

Under P1–P4, the specified one-dimensional internal geometry supports a countably infinite family of nonzero, distinguishable standing-mode types with an explicit phase-safe readout and exact persistence under isolated evolution. The complete dynamics is stable in the proved energy-state norm. P5 supplies a fully numerical matched-action example and its calculated energy differences. Under P6, the geometric overlap coefficients and work identities give a concrete transition interface with explicit conservation accounting. The flavor-space construction required by Step 1.3 of the construction sequence is conditionally constructed and verified.

These are the proved results traced to their premises and finite checks above.
